title: Does the classical Hénon map have a periodic sink?
credit: Hénon (1976); open question as framed by Galias & Tucker (2015)
premise_risks: A positive answer could come from a pure computer search (a certified long-period sink). That is a legitimate solution, but some reviewers may see it as computational.
A negative answer is far beyond current techniques, so the problem may sit open for a long time either way.
plain: The Hénon map H(x,y) = (1 − 1.4x² + y, 0.3x) is the textbook example of a 'strange attractor': on a computer screen its orbits trace out a fractal set. No one has proved that what we see is not just a stable periodic orbit with a very long period. Decide whether H has an attracting periodic orbit.
math: Let $H(x,y)=(1-\tfrac{7}{5}x^2+y,\ \tfrac{3}{10}x)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Decide whether there exist $n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $H^n(p)=p$ such that both eigenvalues of $DH^n(p)$ have modulus $<1$.
